examples.problem_statement: If the heights of two cones are in the ratio 1 : 4 and their diameters are in the ratio 4 : 5, what is the ratio of their volumes ?

solution.result: Volume depends on r^2 and h
solution.description: Write down the cone volume formula the book starts from, so you can see which measurements the volume is sensitive to: the radius squared and the height.

solution.result: Ratio of volumes = (ratio of diameters)^2 \times (ratio of heights)
solution.description: Turn the formula into a ratio statement: the constant \frac{1}{3}\pi cancels, so substitute the given diameter ratio 4 : 5 in place of the radius ratio (diameters scale exactly like radii) and the height ratio 1 : 4.
Square the diameter ratio on its own first, because the radius enters the volume formula squared.
Multiply that squared diameter ratio by the height ratio to finish, and read the resulting fraction back as a ratio.

key_reminders: Cone volume is V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h, so volume scales with the square of the radius and the first power of the height.
Ratio of volumes = (ratio of radii or diameters)^2 \times (ratio of heights).
Diameters may be used in place of radii in the ratio, since d = 2r and the factor 2 cancels.
common_mistakes: Squaring the height ratio 1 : 4 instead of the diameter ratio 4 : 5.
Halving 4 : 5 to get radii before squaring, an unnecessary step that invites arithmetic slips.
Multiplying 16 : 25 by 4 rather than by \frac{1}{4}, which reverses the height ratio.

examples.problem_statement: In a certain barter system, one sack of rice can be traded for two and a half chickens or a third of a medallion. Quantity A: The value of a chicken in sacks of rice. Quantity B: The value of a medallion in sacks of rice.

solution.description: Invert the medallion rate: if one sack buys only a third of a medallion, buying the whole medallion takes three sacks, so Quantity B has the exact value 3.

solution.result: One chicken is worth less than one sack
solution.description: Read the chicken rate the same way: a single sack fetches 2.5 chickens, so each chicken must be worth less than a whole sack of rice.
Bound Quantity A rather than computing it exactly, as the book does: the value of one chicken in sacks of rice is less than 1, which is all the comparison needs.
Compare the bound with the exact value: anything below 1 is below 3, so Quantity B wins without any further calculation.

key_reminders: A rate stated as "one X trades for n Y" inverts to "one Y is worth \frac{1}{n} of an X".
In quantitative comparison, a bound on one quantity is enough when it cannot overlap the other quantity's value.
common_mistakes: Reading "a third of a medallion" as three medallions per sack, which would make Quantity B equal to \frac{1}{3}.
Taking a chicken to be worth 2.5 sacks instead of \frac{1}{2.5} of a sack by failing to invert the rate.
Spending time computing the exact value 0.4 for Quantity A when a bound below 1 already settles it.

concept.sub_category: Calendar - finding the day of the week

examples.problem_statement: Mahatma Gandhi was born on 2 Oct 1869. The day of the week was: 1) Friday 2) Thursday 3) Saturday 4) Monday 5) None of these

solution.description: Break the elapsed time into blocks and take the first block: a complete span of 1600 years contributes 0 odd days, so it can be dropped from the count.
Take the next block of 200 years: each century of the pair carries 5 odd days, giving 10, which reduces to 3 odd days after removing complete weeks.
Handle the leftover 68 years by splitting them into 17 leap years worth 2 odd days each and 51 ordinary years worth 1 each; the total 85 reduces to 1 odd day.
Count the days elapsed within 1869 itself, from 1 January through 2 October, by adding the month lengths and the 2 days of October; 275 reduces to 2 odd days.
Add the odd days from all four blocks and map the total onto the week: 6 odd days lands on Saturday.

key_reminders: An ordinary year carries 1 odd day and a leap year 2 odd days; 400 years carry 0.
Counting by centuries, 100 years carry 5 odd days, so 200 years carry 10, reducing to 3.
Odd days are the remainder after removing whole weeks, so any total is reduced modulo 7 before reading off the day.
common_mistakes: Including 1869 itself in the 68-year block instead of counting its days separately up to 2 October.
Adding 29 for February 1869, which is not a leap year, when totalling the 275 days.
Forgetting to reduce 10 odd days for the 200-year block down to 3, or 85 down to 1.
